doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: What he wants from a bass player
summary: He lists bass-playing friends and wants a big beat and trustworthy time and form.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well sort of a connected question, what do you like to get from a bass player?

Interesting question. Because a lot of my very very best friends are bass players. Yeah because I really love bass. One of my best friends, Jeff Campbell at the Eastman School is beautiful bass player. But I’ve known guys, well John Clayton is a great bass player and he’s one of my heroes and a guy named Bob Bowman in Kansas City a guy that I was on Buddy’s band with, Tom Warrington, and a friend of mine in school named

George Anderson — all these guys were bass players. So I guess just a big beat and someone you can really trust in terms of the time and the form. Because there’s so much, especially in more modern music there’s so much responsibility to a bass player. Because he’s really in charge — to me he’s in charge of the beat and he’s in charge of the harmony, which means he’s in charge of the form. Like Rufus Reid, when he’s playing, he’s in charge of the rhythm section you know? So he wouldn’t say that, but he is. So that’s kind of, I love, and there’s the roots, and I love bass players. I do a lot of playing with chordless trios, with just bass and drums. And I just like a big beat and I love it when they’re so trustworthy in terms of the form.
